questions.question_text: Learned helplessness has been invoked to explain the aetiology of
questions.explanation: Learned helplessness is an apathetic condition in an animal or human resulting from exposure to insoluble problems or inescapable physical or emotional stress, believed by some psychologists to underlie depression. For example, when dogs in a laboratory are exposed to electrical shocks from which they cannot escape, they show behaviours that differentiate them from dogs not exposed to such uncontrollable events. The dogs exposed to the shocks will not cross a barrier to stop the flow of electric shock when put in a new learning situation. They remain passive and do not move. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015. Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 399.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a projective test of personality?
questions.explanation: Projective tests of personality include the Rorschach test, Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), Sentence Completion Test, Holtzman Inkblot Technique (HIT), Figure drawing (typically human forms but can involve houses or other forms) and Make-a-Picture Story (MAPS). Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 59.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is correct concerning people with Type B personalities?

options.text: They may be high achievers and workaholics
They cope poorly when under stress
They show high competitiveness, hostility, and aggression
They show impatience and are incapable of relaxation

correct_answer.text: They cope poorly when under stress

correct_answers.text: They cope poorly when under stress

questions.explanation: Type A persons show impatience, excessive time consciousness, insecurity, high competitiveness, hostility and aggression and are incapable of relaxation. They may be high achievers and workaholics. Type B persons are relaxed, and easy-going, creative, often self-analyze and evade stress but cope poorly when under stress.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following cannot be consciously inspected?
questions.explanation: Non-declarative memory is memory for non-declarative knowledge, involving memory systems that do not draw on the individual's general knowledge. Non-declarative knowledge does not involve awareness and understanding of factual information about the world. It includes procedural knowledge (information about how to carry out sequences of operations – knowing how in contrast to knowing that). It cannot be consciously inspected and does not involve conscious recollection of a previous experience. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: The storage of information in pure form without specification of time and place is called
questions.explanation: Semantic memory is an important part of declarative memory and is concerned with remembering facts, ideas and concepts. It refers to what is known rather than when and how the knowledge was acquired. Eg in answering a question 'what is the capital of Scotland', one is using semantic memory. Most abstract knowledge consists of material drawn from semantic memory (Ref: Psychological basis of psychiatry; Thambirajah- 162)

questions.question_text: In Pavlov's original classical conditioning experiments on dogs, which of the following served as the conditioned stimulus?
questions.explanation: In Pavlov's experiments the food is the unconditioned stimulus because it unconditionally elicits salivation before the experiment begins. The bell is the conditioned stimulus because it only elicits the salivary response conditional on the food-bell pairings. The new response to the bell is correspondingly called the conditioned response, and the natural response to the food itself is the unconditioned response. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1014.

questions.question_text: If the conditioned stimulus (CS) ends prior to the application of unconditioned stimulus (UCS) it is called
questions.explanation: In forward or delayed conditioning, the CS is presented before the UCS and remains on while the UCS is presented until the UCR appears. In backward conditioning, the CS is presented after the UCS and widely used in advertising. In higher order conditioning, a new conditioned stimulus is paired with the old conditioned stimulus and the latter thus effectively acts as an unconditioned stimulus. Trace conditioning and higher order conditioning tends to be fairly weak than delayed conditioning.

questions.question_text: All of the following are true with respect to coping process when faced with a life stressor except

options.text: In emotion-focused coping the individual alters his emotional self-appraisal to the stressful situation
During primary appraisal the individual evaluates his resources to cope
In problem-focused coping the individual attempts to change the stressful situation
Individuals employ a variety of different strategies to cope
There is no universally best strategy for coping

correct_answer.text: During primary appraisal the individual evaluates his resources to cope

correct_answers.text: During primary appraisal the individual evaluates his resources to cope

questions.explanation: Primary appraisal - the individual evaluates the stressor. Secondary appraisal - the individual evaluates his resources and options available to manage the stressful situation.

questions.question_text: A 55-year-old heavy alcoholic was admitted to the medical ward after sustaining a major fall. He has severe anterograde amnesia and extensive retrograde memory loss. However his working memory and procedural memory are unimpaired. What is his most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Korsakoff syndrome is characterised by absence or significant impairment in the ability to lay down new memories, together with a variable length of retrograde amnesia. Working memory is unimpaired, as it procedural and 'emotional' memory. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 606-607.

questions.question_text: A person cannot have two opposing physiological states at the same time. For example, it is not possible to be relaxed and anxious simultaneously. In learning theory, this notion is called
questions.explanation: The behavioral principle of reciprocal inhibition (Wolpe) states that anxiety and relaxation cannot coexist. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 908.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following statements is false about modelling?

options.text: Modelling can also lead to social facilitation and can result in skilled behaviour
Modelling can increase the pain threshold and anxiety threshold
Observational learning is more likely to occur if the model has some characteristics in common with the observer
Modelling refers to the learning that takes place spontaneously by observing the behaviour of another person

correct_answer.text: Modelling can increase the pain threshold and anxiety threshold

correct_answers.text: Modelling can increase the pain threshold and anxiety threshold

questions.explanation: Modelling can also lead to social facilitation, can result in skilled behaviour, can lower the pain threshold and anxiety threshold. Observational learning is more likely to occur if the model has some characteristics in common with the observer. Other Effective models for observational learning include competency of the model, perceived high status and possess social influence or power.

questions.question_text: In a Pavlovian conditioning paradigm, the bell was rung before the food was presented and the bell continued till salivation appeared. This is called
questions.explanation: In Pavlov's experiments the food is the unconditioned stimulus because it unconditionally elicits salivation before the experiment begins. The bell is known as the conditioned stimulus because it only elicits the salivary response conditional on the food-bell pairings. Forward conditioning is the usual method of classical conditioning, in which the conditioned stimulus precedes the unconditioned stimulus. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1014. Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Raven's progressive matrices test is used to assess
questions.explanation: The Raven's Progressive Matrices (RPM) is a non-verbal test that is widely used to assess 'general cognitive ability'. Three different versions of the RPM exist: the Raven standard progressive matrices (RSPM), the coloured progressive matrices (which is easier), and the advanced progressive matrices (which is more difficult). The original 60-item RSPM is the most frequently used version and can be used for all age groups. Each item shows a geometric pattern with a missing piece. Participants must select the correct answer option that completes the pattern. Ref: Langener A et al. A shortened version of Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices for children and adolescents. Br J Dev Psych. 2021:1-11.

questions.question_text: The brain region thought to be responsible for majority of working memory functions is
questions.explanation: Working memory is a temporary store for recently activated items of information that are currently occupying consciousness and that can be manipulated and moved in and out of short-term memory. Its functions are carried out largely in the prefrontal cortex of the brain. The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, in particular, has been strongly implicated in working memory. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Cognitive processing during social learning includes all except
questions.explanation: Cognitive processing during social learning involves various domains: 1. Attention to observed behaviour is the basic element in learning. 2. Visual image and semantic encoding of observed behaviour memory 3. Memory permanence via retention and rehearsal 4. Motor copying of the behaviour and imitative reproduction 5. Motivation to act.

questions.question_text: Which conditioning is involved in the aetiology of both agoraphobia and of obsessional rituals?
questions.explanation: The term aversive conditioning refers to situations in which behavior is motivated by the threat of an unpleasant stimulus. There are two main categories of behavior under aversive control: avoidance behavior and escape behavior. Escape conditioning occurs when the animal learns to perform an operant to terminate an ongoing, aversive stimulus. It is a "get me out of here" or "shut this off" reaction, aimed at escape from pain. The behavior that produces escape is negatively reinforced (reinforced by the elimination of the unpleasant stimulus). For example, the jump of a rat from electrified platform onto a bowl of water is an escape behavior. Escape conditioning is converted into avoidance conditioning by giving a signal before the aversive stimulus starts. If the animal receives a cue or signal that an aversive stimulus is coming, then after one or two occurrences of the punishing stimulus the cue will trigger an avoidance behavior. This kind of learning occurs quickly and is very durable. For example, if you sounded a tone before you electrified the platform, after one or two trials the rat would respond to the tone by jumping into the water. It would not wait for the shock. Avoidance behaviors are very persistent even when there is no longer anything to avoid. The reason is that as a result of an avoidance reaction, one never experiences the aversive stimulus. But this serves as a negative reinforcement, providing a sense of relief. Because of this, avoidance behavior is self-reinforcing. (Excerpt from Avoidance and Escape Learning, Chapter 5: Conditioning, http://www.intropsych.com/ch05_conditioning/avoidance_and_escape_learning.html (accessed April 13, 2015))

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a feature of Type A personality?
questions.explanation: Type A personality is characterised by hurried activity, impatience, ambition, and competitiveness. It is generally associated with the AHA triad of traits (anger, hostility, and aggression). The term was introduced by US cardiologists Meyer Friedman and Ray Harold Rosenman. They presented the first evidence indicating a significantly increased risk of coronary heart disease associated with Type A behaviour. Type B persons are relaxed and easy-going, creative, often self-analyze and evade stress, but cope poorly when under stress. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Compulsions provide short-term relief of obsessional anxiety. The learning principle operating here is
questions.explanation: In operant conditioning, negative reinforcement refers to the strengthening of a response (in this example, a compulsion) as a consequence of its being followed by the cessation or avoidance of an aversive stimulus (in this example, anxiety cued by obsessions). When practicing compulsive rituals, anxiety is acutely reduced. This provides a reinforcement to practice the compulsions repeatedly. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following can test abstract reasoning?
questions.explanation: The Goldstein-Scheerer test are a set of tests requiring abstract thinking and concept formation, used to diagnose neurological damage. The tests require the respondent to copy coloured designs, to sort items into categories according to colour, form, and material, and to reproduce designs from memory by arranging sticks. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a part of the Big Five personality traits?
questions.explanation: The 'big five' personality traits (Costa and McCrae) are: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism (OCEAN). Ref: Franić S, Borsboom D, Dolan CV, Boomsma DI. The big five personality traits: Psychological entities or statistical constructs?. Behavior genetics. 2014 Nov;44(6):591-604.

questions.question_text: Of all sensory systems, the system least developed at birth is
questions.explanation: Of all the senses, sight is the least developed at birth; visual acuity in newborns is about 20/300

questions.question_text: When carried out in imagination, immediate exposure to elements at the top of the hierarchy without any gradation of anxiety-inducing stimuli is termed as
questions.explanation: By exposing the patient to the phobic object and preventing the usual escape or avoidance, there is extinction of the usual (maladaptive) anxiety response. This may be done in vivo (flooding) or in imagination (implosion). Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 908.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes flash-bulb memories?

options.text: Memories of events that happened in broad day-light persisting for longer periods of time
Vivid memories of personal events associated with intense emotional arousal
Instantaneous recall that cannot be sustained for further processing
Recall of images in memory with extreme accuracy and in abundant volume
Instances of knowing something that cannot immediately be recalled

correct_answer.text: Vivid memories of personal events associated with intense emotional arousal

correct_answers.text: Vivid memories of personal events associated with intense emotional arousal

questions.explanation: Flashbulb memories are a specific type of autobiographical memory in which the person becomes aware of an emotionally arousing event, for example, the 9/11 terrorist bombings. Even though they are recalled with seeming accuracy due to rehearsal, their accuracy cannot be assumed. Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish's clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 63.

questions.question_text: Mr. Y has amnesia following traumatic brain injury involving the hippocampus. Which of the following would be spared?
questions.explanation: The performance of tasks such as typing, swimming, or cutting a loaf of bread are expressions of prior learning that differ from episodic memory in that there is no active awareness that memory is being searched in undertaking the particular skill. This type of memory is known as implicit, procedural, or skills memory. Studies of people with injury to the hippocampus suggest that declarative and implicit memory use different parts of the brain and can function independently. The hippocampus is believed to be the site where explicit (declarative) memory is stored, while implicit (procedural) memory is thought to reside in the limbic system, the amygdala, and the cerebellum. Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish's clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 64.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a component of the Big Five Theory of personality?
questions.explanation: The 'big five' personality traits are: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism (OCEAN). They include: 1. Extraversion which encompasses more specific traits as talkative, energetic, and assertiveness. 2. Agreeableness which includes sympathetic, kind and affectionate approach. 3. Conscientiousness that includes traits such as being organized, thorough, and planful. 4. Neuroticism which includes traits like being tense, moody and anxious. 5. Openness to Experience which includes traits like having wide interests, being imaginative and insightful. Ref: Franić S, Borsboom D, Dolan CV, Boomsma DI. The big five personality traits: Psychological entities or statistical constructs?. Behavior genetics. 2014 Nov;44(6):591-604.

questions.question_text: The concept of motivated forgetting is based on the psychoanalytic concept of
questions.explanation: Motivated forgetting (or catathymic amnesia) is the inability to recall specific painful/traumatic memories and is believed to occur due to the defence mechanism of repression. Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish's clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 65.

questions.question_text: Mr. Z visited his doctor and following his visit he remembered the first few things he had been told better than subsequent information. What is the name of this tendency?
questions.explanation: In serial learning, the primacy effect is a tendency for the items near the beginning of the series to be better recalled than those near the middle. Also items that are presented towards the end of the list are more likely to be remembered, which is called the recency effect. Primacy is supposed to be due to LTM as consolidation has occurred in the sufficient time between learning the first word and testing recall. Recency is due to STM where last heard words are freshly retained. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following statements is true?

options.text: Positive reinforcement reduces the likelihood of a behaviour occurring
Negative reinforcement reduces the likelihood of a behaviour occurring
Intermittent reinforcement schedules result in acquired behaviours that are more resistant to extinction than behaviours induced by continuous reinforcement
Partial reinforcement leads to rapid acquisition and slower extinction of a response
In negative reinforcement, presentation of an aversive stimulus weakens the response

correct_answer.text: Intermittent reinforcement schedules result in acquired behaviours that are more resistant to extinction than behaviours induced by continuous reinforcement

correct_answers.text: Intermittent reinforcement schedules result in acquired behaviours that are more resistant to extinction than behaviours induced by continuous reinforcement

questions.explanation: In operant conditioning, reinforcement refers to any stimulus that, if it is presented soon after a response, increases the relative frequency with which that response is emitted in the future. Reinforcement can be positive (behaviour is followed by a desirable outcome) or negative (behaviour is followed by removal of an aversive stimulus). It can occur after every response (continuous reinforcement) or only after some responses (partial or intermittent reinforcement). Intermittent reinforcement can generate high rates of behaviour that are resistant to extinction, as seen in behaviour directed at a casino slot machine. Behaviours conditioned by partial reinforcement are acquired more slowly and extinguish at a much slower rate than those conditioned by continuous reinforcement. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 907. Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1018.

questions.question_text: Mr. X was admitted to an intensive medical care unit following a severe head injury. On formal cognitive testing, he was unable to recall salient experiences in the days and weeks before the injury. What type of amnesia is this?
questions.explanation: Retrograde amnesia is loss of memory for events or experience before a traumatic event or incident that causes the amnesia. Many patients may have lost the ability to form or retain new episodic memories, a condition called anterograde amnesia. Transient global amnesia is caused by transient cerebral ischaemia causing a temporary lack of blood supply to the regions of the brain concerned with memory functions. The main features include sudden onset of severe anterograde amnesia with a retrograde amnesia for the preceding days or weeks. Sometimes amnesic episodes may occur in patients who have had no brain injury but who have suffered a traumatic or emotionally disturbing life event, and it is called hysterical amnesia. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Mr. X is seen in the psychiatric outpatient clinic, complaining of 'absent-mindedness'. He says that he intends to take his medications and keep appointments, but he repeatedly forgets. This is likely due to
questions.explanation: Failure of prospective memory is a common cause of 'absent-mindedness'. Prospective memory is defined as the memory for intentions. It enables us to carry out an action that has been planned for a predefined time in the future, while performing a concurrent activity (ongoing task). Retrieving an intention entails remembering at the right moment that something has to be done (prospective component) and remembering what has to be done. Ref: Lecouvey G et al. An impairment of prospective memory in mild Alzheimer's disease: a ride in a virtual town. Frontiers in psychology. 2019 Feb 12;10:241.

questions.question_text: A reinforced operant response weakens when the reinforcement is ceased. This is called
questions.explanation: Extinction is the diminution in the strength or frequency of a conditioned response as a result of its having been elicited repeatedly without reinforcement. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: In a behavioural technique, actual exposure to a feared stimulus takes place for a substantial amount of time, so the accompanying anxiety response fades away. This is called
questions.explanation: By exposing the patient to the phobic object and preventing the usual escape or avoidance, there is extinction of the usual (maladaptive) anxiety response. This may be done in vivo (flooding) or in imagination (implosion). Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 908.

questions.question_text: George has a history of anxiety disorder. On visiting a church, he developed a sense of familiarity because his stored memories were brought into his consciousness. This phenomenon is called
questions.explanation: Recognition is the act or process of perceiving or identifying information as matching or being the same as information that has been remembered. It is often contrasted with 'recall' which involves reproduction of remembered information without cues. Recognition is generally easier than recall. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Timeout refers to a technique that is aimed at
questions.explanation: Time out or loss of privileges are used as negative reinforcement strategies to reduce unwanted behaviours in children

questions.question_text: Information is held in the long term memory by the process of
questions.explanation: Elaborative rehearsal is the deep processing of material that needs to be remembered, involving formation of associations, organisation (regrouping of material into categories), use of mnemonic strategies, or other forms of cognitive processing. In contrast, maintenance rehearsal is the simple repetition (without elaboration) of items that need to be remembered in order to prevent them from fading from short-term memory (as when a person repeats a phone number over and over while searching for a pen and paper to write it down). Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is correct concerning sensory memory? Sensory memory has

options.text: Small capacity but memories are unprocessed and of long duration (>0.5s)
Small capacity and memories are unprocessed and of very short duration (<0.5s)
Large capacity but memories are unprocessed and of very short duration (<0.5s)
Large capacity but memories are unprocessed and of long duration (>0.5s)
Large capacity but memories are processed and of very short duration (<0.5s)

correct_answer.text: Large capacity but memories are unprocessed and of very short duration (<0.5s)

correct_answers.text: Large capacity but memories are unprocessed and of very short duration (<0.5s)

questions.explanation: Sensory memory is a very short-term large-capacity memory store for information being processed by the sense organs. It has a large capacity, but objects are unprocessed. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following test is a measure of nonverbal intelligence?
questions.explanation: The Raven's Progressive Matrices (RPM) is a non-verbal test that is widely used to assess 'general cognitive ability'. Three different versions of the RPM exist: the Raven standard progressive matrices (RSPM), the coloured progressive matrices (which is easier), and the advanced progressive matrices (which is more difficult). The original 60-item RSPM is the most frequently used version and can be used for all age groups. Each item shows a geometric pattern with a missing piece. Participants must select the correct answer option that completes the pattern. Ref: Langener A et al. A shortened version of Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices for children and adolescents. Br J Dev Psych. 2021:1-11.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a way of measuring personality along the dimensions of extroversion-introversion and neuroticism-stability?
questions.explanation: The Eysenck Personality Inventory is a questionnaire designed to measure two major dimensions of personality, namely extraversion and neuroticism, according to the theory of personality propounded by the German-born British psychologist Hans Eysenck. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: A good test for recent memory is to ask patients which of the following?

options.text: What they had to eat for their last meal
Who is the prime minister of UK

correct_answer.text: What they had to eat for their last meal

correct_answers.text: What they had to eat for their last meal

questions.explanation: Recent memory is the ability to remember what has been experienced within the past few minutes (Recall of items after five minutes), hours (Recall of last meal), days (Recall of recent topics in news). Remote memory is the ability to remember events in the distant past (weeks to years). This can be tested by inquiring about important dates in their lives such as date of birth, date of marriage and how many siblings they have.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is not one of the Gestalt principles of perception?
questions.explanation: The Gestalt principles of perception would include proximity, closure, similarity, continuity and symmetry. According to Gestalt principles, we tend to perceive whole objects rather than parts. The perceptual system in our brains employs these principles to enable us perceive unified forms rather than simple collections of unconnected images.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true regarding processes that govern formation of various types of memory?

options.text: Attention allows decoding long term memory store
Lack of attention leads to forgetting
Attention allows short-term memory to enter long-term memory store
Attention allows sensory memory to enter short term memory store
Lack of attention leads to delay in recall

correct_answer.text: Attention allows sensory memory to enter short term memory store

correct_answers.text: Attention allows sensory memory to enter short term memory store

questions.explanation: Attention is a key process that enables sensory memory traces to enter into short term memory.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is a secondary emotion according to Plutchik?
questions.explanation: Plutchik proposed a list eight basic (primary) emotions. They were matched in four bipolar dyads of dissimilar states that do not occur in the human mind at the same time: anticipation-surprise, joy-sadness, acceptance-disgust, and anger-fear. When two or more basic emotions are combined, a new emotional state (secondary emotion) emerges. For example, joy and anticipation blend to give emerging optimism, a mix of surprise and sadness results in disappointment, and love is a combination of joy and acceptance. Ref: Imbir K.K. (2017) Psychoevolutionary Theory of Emotion (Plutchik). In: Zeigler-Hill V., Shackelford T. (eds) Encyclopedia of Personality and Individual Differences. Springer, Cham. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-28099-8_547-1

questions.question_text: Which of the following tests can be used to determine pre-morbid intelligence of a 70-year-old coal miner who shows signs of cognitive impairment?

options.text: Wechsler's Adult Intelligence Test - block design subtest

questions.explanation: First published in 1982, the 50-item National Adult Reading Test (NART) is a widely adopted method for estimating premorbid intelligence both for clinical and research purposes. Ref: Bright P et al. The National Adult Reading Test: restandardisation against the Wechsler adult intelligence scale—fourth edition. Neuropsychological Rehabilitation. 2018 Aug 18;28(6):1019-27.

questions.question_text: A rat receives positive reinforcement (a food pellet) for pressing a bar that turns on a red light, but not an adjacent bar that turns on a green light. The process that best explains this is
questions.explanation: The basic principles of operant conditioning are that if a response to a stimulus produces positive consequences for the individual, it will tend to be repeated, while if it is followed by negative consequences, it will not. In Thorndike and Skinner's original experiments, rats were placed in a box containing a level that, when pressed, delivered a pellet of food. Eventually, the rat would press the lever and be rewarded. The rat would then press the lever with increasing frequency. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 907.

questions.question_text: Which of the following theorists proposed six basic emotions?
questions.explanation: A widely accepted theory of basic emotions and their expression, developed by Paul Ekman, suggests that humans have six basic emotions: anger, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, and surprise. These emotions combine in different ways to form other emotions, including compassion, boredom, embarrassment, rage, hunger, and more. Ref: Sauter DA et al. Cross-cultural recognition of basic emotions through nonverbal emotional vocalizations. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 2010 Feb 9;107(6):2408-12.

questions.question_text: In studies on arousal levels related to different emotions, which emotion produces the maximum rise in temperature compared to all other emotions;
questions.explanation: Anger- maximum rise in temperature. Fear and Disgust- drop in temperature. Studies on emotions have shown that the heart rate increase produced by sadness is usually greater than that produced by happiness.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is not correctly paired?
questions.explanation: Social learning refers to the processes by which social influences alter people's thoughts, feelings, and behaviour. Albert Bandura argued that imitation and modelling can occur without reinforcement, through simple observational learning, as in an experiment by Bandura and two colleagues in which children who observed the actions of an aggressive adult towards an inflatable five-foot BoBo doll tended later, after they were subjected to mild frustration, to imitate the hostile behaviour they had observed. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which one of Maslow's hierarchy of needs represents the need to develop a sense of personal worth and competence and the need for recognition by others?
questions.explanation: Abraham Maslow proposed a need-hierarchy theory. According to Maslow, the strongest and most imperative are the physiological needs for food, water, oxygen, and sex. If the physiological needs are gratified, the needs for safety emerge, and the person begins to seek out safe environments. Next to emerge are needs for love and belonging, and the person yearns for a friend, a lover, a place in a group. Then needs for esteem come to the fore, and the person seeks self-respect, respect from others, status, and achievement. Then last, usually only if all the others have been reasonably well-satisfied, there emerges a need for self-actualisation. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Tip of the tongue state is a well investigated example of
questions.explanation: The 'ugly sister effect' is a common feature of the 'tip-of-the-tongue' (TOT) phenomenon, when a different but related blocking memory pops into consciousness, impeding access to the required memory, and generally being difficult or impossible to dislodge. (The 'ugly sister' alludes to the fairy tale in which the prince tries to gain access to the beautiful Cinderella but is blocked by her ugly sisters, who pop up in her place.) Blocking is said to occur when subjects are unable to access information that they know exists in their memory despite great efforts at recalling, even in the presence of retrieval cues. TOT states may last for few seconds or for a few days. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: The commonest cause of long-term forgetting is

options.text: Failure in encoding at the time of the input
Failure of transfer of information from short term to long term memory
Failure of transfer of information from long term to short term memory
Failure in encoding at the time of retrieval

questions.explanation: The cause of long-term forgetting may be due to; Failure in encoding at the time of the input, failure of transfer of information from short-term to long term memory and retrieval failure (more commonly).

questions.question_text: 'People can only attend to one physical channel of information at a time.' Which theory of attention states this?

options.text: Shiffrin and Schneider's divided attention theory

questions.explanation: The filter theory of attention, proposed by the English psychologist David Broadbent, states that there exists a central processor with a limited capacity that can select only one sensory input channel at a time. It can switch no more than about twice per second, while information in an unattended channel is held in short-term memory for a few seconds. Broadbent proposed that a filter lies between the sensory buffer and short-term store (what is now called working memory) that prevents overloading memory. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: A 24 year old woman develops significant fear of driving after having a relatively trivial road traffic collision. She avoids using cars even as a passenger. She has no symptoms of PTSD. Which of the following therapies is best suited for her needs?
questions.explanation: This is simple phobia for driving and not PTSD. So behaviour therapy is the correct option.

questions.question_text: Which of the following describes Eysenck's model of personality traits?
questions.explanation: Eysenck's theory is also called the three-factor theory or the P-E-N theory. The three higher-order factors are extraversion-introversion; neuroticism-stability and psychoticism-impulse control. His work asserts that the P-E-N dimensions are biologically based and largely heritable.

questions.question_text: Increase in the strength of the response following brief but repeated exposure to the stimulus is called
questions.explanation: Incubation refers to increase in the strength of a response following brief but repeated exposures to a stimulus. Extinction occurs when the conditioned stimulus is repeatedly presented in the absence of the unconditioned stimulus. It is a concept in classical conditioning. It can be delayed by random reinforcement during the acquisition phase. In habituation, the successive presentation of a stimulus, which elicits a response eventually, leads to decrease in the intensity of that response. Stimulus generalisation is a concept in classical conditioning. It refers to the process by which CR gets generalised to other stimuli that are similar to the CS. The fear that a child with a spider phobia shows towards insects is an example of stimulus generalisation. Humans are biologically predisposed to react with fear to certain stimuli. This is stimulus preparedness and here conditioning occurs more quickly and more resistant to extinction in the case of such prepared stimuli e.g. snake phobias.

questions.question_text: Digit span test is administered to a patient with suspected cognitive impairment. Normal reverse digit span in a working age adult is
questions.explanation: Normal forward span is 7 ± 2 digits; while the normal reverse span is 5 ± 2 digits.

questions.question_text: The memories closest to a disruptive event are most vulnerable to loss. This is called
questions.explanation: Ribot's law is the principle that, during retrograde amnesia, the oldest memories are most resistant to disruption or impairment. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following statements regarding perception is incorrect?

options.text: The perceptual set is determined by factors both in the perceiver and in the stimulus
The perceptual set is influenced by emotions
'Perceptual set' is the perceptual bias that predisposes the perceiver to notice only certain aspects of a stimulus and to ignore the other aspects.
The perceptual set is influenced by past experiences
Perceptual set predisposes the perceiver to notice all aspects of a stimulus simultaneously

correct_answer.text: Perceptual set predisposes the perceiver to notice all aspects of a stimulus simultaneously

correct_answers.text: Perceptual set predisposes the perceiver to notice all aspects of a stimulus simultaneously

questions.explanation: The perceptual set is a temporary readiness or predisposition to perceive in a particular way. It does not predispose the perceiver to notice all aspects of a stimulus simultaneously. The perceptual set is determined by factors both in the perceiver and in the stimulus. Factors include the threshold for perception (eg cocktail party phenomenon), personality, past experience, emotions (anxious people biased towards perception of threat-related stimuli), individual values (children exaggerate the size of coins), current drive state and environment (Inuit recognise 100 different kinds of snow). Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: The traits included in 'big five' theory include all except
questions.explanation: The 'big five' personality traits are: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism (OCEAN). Ref: Franić S, Borsboom D, Dolan CV, Boomsma DI. The big five personality traits: Psychological entities or statistical constructs?. Behavior genetics. 2014 Nov;44(6):591-604.

questions.question_text: Which is a form of negative reinforcement used in the treatment of alcohol dependence?
questions.explanation: Disulfiram is often described as 'aversive' and disulfiram treatment is often confused with aversion therapy. However, aversion therapy involves repeated exposure to an unpleasant stimulus. Most disulfiram patients never experience the disulfiram-ethanol reaction and do not need to in order for disulfiram to be effective. Negative reinforcement of abstinence occurs when patients find that adherence to disulfiram (which can be aided by supervised administration) reduces the anxiety normally caused by internal conflicts about drinking vs not drinking that typically occur many times a day. Ref: Brewer C et al. Supervised disulfiram's superior effectiveness in alcoholism treatment: ethical, methodological, and psychological aspects. Alcohol and Alcoholism. 2017 Mar 9;52(2):213-9.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following statements regarding needs and motivation is incorrect?

options.text: According to Yerkes-Dodson curve, there is an inverted U-shaped relationship between arousal (motivation) and performance level
According to Cannon's homeostatic theory, changes in homeostatic system triggers processes aimed at restoration of system
According to Maslow's hierarchy of needs, needs at the previous level need to be satisfied before one can progress to the next level
According to drive reduction theory, the motivation of behaviour is to decrease the arousal associated with basic drives
In Maslow's hierarchy of needs, cognitive needs precede esteem needs

correct_answer.text: In Maslow's hierarchy of needs, cognitive needs precede esteem needs

correct_answers.text: In Maslow's hierarchy of needs, cognitive needs precede esteem needs

questions.explanation: Abraham Maslow proposed a need-hierarchy theory. According to Maslow, the strongest and most imperative are the physiological needs for food, water, oxygen, and sex. If the physiological needs are gratified, the needs for safety emerge, and the person begins to seek out safe environments. Next to emerge are needs for love and belonging, and the person yearns for a friend, a lover, a place in a group. Then needs for esteem come to the fore, and the person seeks self-respect, respect from others, status, and achievement. Then last, usually only if all the others have been reasonably well-satisfied, there emerges a need for self-actualisation. The five-stage model was later expanded to include additional growth needs: cognitive needs and aesthetic needs (right below self-actualization), and transcendence needs (above self-actualisation). Cannon postulated the homeostatic drive theory. According to this theory, changes in homeostatic system trigger processes aimed at restoration of system. Basic needs (biological needs), being self-regulating, function homeostatically. According to Yerkes-Dodson curve, there is an inverted U-shaped relationship between arousal (motivation) and performance level. As the level of emotional arousal increases, so does performance efficiency, to an optimum level. As the emotional arousal increases above this point, performance starts to deteriorate In the drive reduction theory by Hull, the motivation of behaviour is to decrease the arousal associated with basic drives (e.g. thirst). But doesn't explain curiosity motives and the theory is generally rejected. Ref: https://www.simplypsychology.org/maslow.html Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following correctly describes the exposure and response prevention treatment for a lady with fear of contamination and repeated washing?

options.text: Therapist asks her too limit her washing to 4 times per act
Therapist asks her to wash her hands without touching the dirt
Therapist asks her to say 'STOP' aloud whenever the fear of contamination is experienced
Therapist asks her to touch the dirty linen but prevents her from washing her hands
Therapist asks her to touch dirty linen before thoroughly washing her hand with antiseptics

correct_answer.text: Therapist asks her to touch the dirty linen but prevents her from washing her hands

correct_answers.text: Therapist asks her to touch the dirty linen but prevents her from washing her hands

questions.explanation: Exposure and response prevention (ERP) is a form of CBT that involves providing psychoeducation to the patient, helping the patient confront fears or discomfort related to their obsessional thoughts (exposure), and having the patient resist performing compulsions (response prevention). Patients can be exposed to actual situations (in vivo exposure), imagined situations (imaginal exposure), or the physical sensations associated with anxiety or discomfort (interoceptive exposure). The goal of ERP is to challenge how a patient responds to distress and to eventually learn that feared stimuli are safe. Ref: Law C, Boisseau CL. Exposure and response prevention in the treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder: Current perspectives. Psychology research and behavior management. 2019;12:1167.

questions.question_text: The strategies to improve encoding includes all except
questions.explanation: Strategies to improve encoding include - order and sorting info, chunking, mnemonics, using imageries, adding importance and salience to the info and using primacy-Recency effects. Retrieval can be helped by cueing and reinstatement of learning context. The more similar the retrieval situation is to the encoding situation, the better retrieval. This is called encoding specificity principle.

questions.question_text: The modification of memories in terms of one's general attitude is called
questions.explanation: Unconscious distortion of memory, as dictated by one's present psychological needs, is called as Retrospective Falsification. People who retrospectively falsify a story also tend to embellish the positive and delete the negative aspects of the situation. Example: During marital conflicts argument ensues over the partners' differing recollections of their original verbal exchanges.

questions.question_text: Which of the following refers to the formation of initial memory traces?
questions.explanation: Encoding is characterised by converting information into a different form or representation, especially (in psychology) the process whereby physical sensory information is transformed into a representation suitable for storage in memory and subsequent retrieval. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: A dysthymic patient vividly recalled the events that occurred when he was depressed but poorly recalled the events that occurred during happier times. This is an example of
questions.explanation: State-dependent memory refers to the tendency for information learnt in a particular mental or physical state to be most easily remembered in a similar state. Emotional states can produce this effect (sometimes called mood-dependent memory) and this helps to explain why pleasant experiences are more likely to be remembered by a person who is happy, and unpleasant experiences by someone who is unhappy and is likely to become even more unhappy as a result. A depressed patient will normally tend to focus on events that happened during periods of depression and will have difficulty recalling more positive moments. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Skinner's operant conditioning is based on which of the following principles?

options.text: An association is learnt without overt behavioural expression
A response gets paired with a consequence
A response gets paired with its probability
A response gets paired with an internal stimulus
A stimulus gets paired with a response

correct_answer.text: A response gets paired with a consequence

correct_answers.text: A response gets paired with a consequence

questions.explanation: The basic principles of operant conditioning are that if a response to a stimulus produces positive consequences for the individual, it will tend to be repeated, while if it is followed by negative consequences, it will not. In Thorndike and Skinner's original experiments, rats were placed in a box containing a level that, when pressed, delivered a pellet of food. Eventually, the rat would press the lever and be rewarded. The rat would then press the lever with increasing frequency. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 907.

questions.question_text: A parrot was given a new cage. When the parrot touched a lever in the cage, it received an electric shock. It did not touch the lever again. The learning process that has occurred here is
questions.explanation: When an action leads to a positive outcome, the action is strengthened. Conversely, when an action leads to a negative outcome, we have 'punishment', and the action is weakened. Punishment is any stimulus that an organism seeks to avoid or escape. Punishment can be either negative or positive, depending on the nature of the consequence. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1014. Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015. p. 623.

questions.question_text: Flynn effect refers to which of the following phenomenon?

options.text: Changes of IQ with cultural variations
If an IQ test is repeated on the same individual the score increases
If IQ of parents is high, then the IQ of the child is high

questions.explanation: The Flynn effect refers to a secular increase in average IQ scores, typically averaging about three IQ points per decade, that has been occurring since the introduction of IQ tests in many industrialised societies, the effect being most pronounced on measures of fluid intelligence such as Raven's Progressive Matrices. Because IQ tests are periodically re-standardised to a mean of 100, the increase is not apparent in continuously rising average IQ scores, but people who score 100 on a newly standardised test tend to score more than 100 on older ones. The effect has been attributed to various causes, including improved nutrition and parenting, better schooling, increased test-taking sophistication, and various effects of growing up with television and video games in an increasingly complex environment, but it is generally acknowledged to be poorly understood and largely mysterious. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: A family has got a new dog. A 3-year-old child in the family is afraid of dogs and would stay in the same room with the dog only if he could sit on his mother's lap and had his favourite ice cream. Select the learning theory principle employed here
questions.explanation: The behavioral principle of reciprocal inhibition (Wolpe) states that anxiety and relaxation cannot coexist. Comfort with mother and ice-cream conflicts with discomfort produced by the dog - eventually the dog stops eliciting discomfort. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 908.

questions.question_text: Which of the following behavioural treatments is useful in trichotillomania?
questions.explanation: Behavioural therapy with habit-reversal training components has demonstrated the largest treatment effects and has the strongest evidence base for reducing trichotillomania symptoms. Ref: Farhat LC et al. Pharmacological and behavioral treatment for trichotillomania: An updated systematic review with meta‐analysis. Depression and anxiety. 2020 Aug;37(8):715-27.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an inaccurate statement concerning sensory memory?

options.text: Each sense has its own sensory memory e.g. iconic (visual), echoic (auditory) etc.
Information is processed in sensory memory
It has a large capacity but gets disrupted by inflow of new information in same modality
Information that is attended to is transferred to short-term memory store and information that is not selected for processing is rapidly lost

correct_answer.text: Information is processed in sensory memory

correct_answers.text: Information is processed in sensory memory

questions.explanation: Sensory memory is a very short-term memory store for information being processed by the sense organs. The most frequently investigated sensory registers are the iconic (visual) store and the echoic (auditory) store. Sensory registers are assumed to exist separately for each sensory modality. No processing is involved in sensory memory. Information that is attended to is transferred to short-term memory store, and information that is not selected for processing is rapidly lost. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: A medical student becomes more comfortable in the anatomy laboratory after several weeks of exposure to it. Which of the following explains this process?
questions.explanation: Habituation is the process of making or becoming used to something. More specifically, it is the diminution in the strength or frequency of an unconditioned response to the stimulus that evokes it. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: A patient has a phobia of escalators and avoids London tube stations as a result. Deep muscle relaxation is paired with a series of imagined scenes that are arranged in a hierarchy from the least to the most anxiety-producing stimuli. This therapy is called
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) is frequently used in the treatment of phobic anxiety disorders. It is based on the behavioural principle of reciprocal inhibition (i.e. anxiety and relaxation cannot coexist). Three steps involve : 1) Relaxation training, 2) Constructing a hierarchy of anxieties, and 3) Desensitisation of the stimulus. The patient is exposed to a graded hierarchy of anxiety-provoking situations in a stepwise fashion while being taught to practice the relaxation techniques (e.g. a young woman with a spider phobia is taught relaxation techniques and then exposed to experiences starting from the lowest level of her hierarchy of anxieties - such as going to the cellar where there is the potential to come across a spider - then progressively going up the ladder to the highest - such as handling a spider). Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 908.

questions.question_text: Amnesic syndrome is characterised by a marked impairment in
questions.explanation: Episodic memory is memory for specific events. Amnesia is defined as partial or total inability to recall past experiences and events. Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish's clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 64.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes Ribot's law in memory disturbances?

options.text: In organic amnesia remote memory content is lost before recent content.
In organic amnesia recent memory content is lost before remote content.
In dissociative amnesia anterograde amnesia is dense.
In organic amnesia anterograde amnesia cannot occur without retrograde loss.
In dissociative amnesia recent memory content is lost before remote content.

correct_answer.text: In organic amnesia recent memory content is lost before remote content.

correct_answers.text: In organic amnesia recent memory content is lost before remote content.

questions.explanation: Ribot's law is the principle that, during retrograde amnesia, the oldest memories are most resistant to disruption or impairment. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Biofeedback can mainly modify which of the following functions?
questions.explanation: Biofeedback involves the transmission to subjects of information about biological functions. It can modify cardiovascular function and is a useful method of reducing muscle tension. It is a technique for controlling physiological responses by receiving information about these responses as they occur. Monitoring devices track physiological responses such as heart rate, blood pressure, and muscle tension and provide the person with feedback in the form of light or tone whenever they change the response in the desired direction. With practice, a person can learn to control all sorts of bodily functions predominantly through relaxation (Excerpt retrieved from http://www.abahe.co.uk/biofeedback-definition.html).

questions.question_text: All of the following are deficiency needs except
questions.explanation: Maslow's hierarchy of needs is a motivation theory in psychology originally comprised of a five-tier model, often depicted as hierarchical levels within a pyramid. From the bottom of the hierarchy upwards, the needs are: physiological, safety, love and belonging, esteem, and self-actualisation. The first four levels are often referred to as deficiency needs, and the top level is known as growth or being needs. The five-stage model was later expanded to include additional growth needs: cognitive needs and aesthetic needs (right below self-actualization), and transcendence needs (above self-actualisation). Ref: https://www.simplypsychology.org/maslow.html

questions.question_text: Which among the following is defined as the basic building block or unit of intelligent behaviour?
questions.explanation: A schema is defined as the basic building block or unit of intelligent behaviour. Schemas consist of organised past experiences to understand future experiences. We have physical schemas such as bike riding schema and mental schemas such as addition, multiplication and division schema

questions.question_text: A clinical psychologist performed digit span test and immediately asked the patient to count a three digit number backwards. What is this procedure called as?
questions.explanation: Under normal situations, the duration for which information is held in short term memory is usually 15 to 20 seconds. STM is also very fragile and information is lost quickly. Brown Paterson demonstrated that by 15 seconds the original material is completely forgotten. Brown Paterson task involves introducing distraction (such as counting a three digit number backwards) immediately after the digit span test in order to prevent rehearsal.

questions.question_text: Which of the following would demonstrate declarative memories?

options.text: Knowledge of how to drive a car
Knowledge of how to ride a bike
Knowledge of capitals of different countries
Knowledge of how to write a letter

correct_answer.text: Knowledge of capitals of different countries

correct_answers.text: Knowledge of capitals of different countries

questions.explanation: Memory for factual knowledge and autobiographical events is collectively termed declarative memory. It supports the conscious recollection of facts and events. Declarative (also known as explicit) memory is of two types: episodic memory or memory for specific events (such as going to the shop this morning) and semantic memory or memory for abstract facts such as the capitals of countries. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 1025, 1027. Casey P, Kelly B. Fish's clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 64.

questions.question_text: A candidate who is attempting his final exam before graduation thinks that he is going to fail the whole exam as he has got one 'obvious question' wrong. He is exhibiting
questions.explanation: Overgeneralisation is cognitive distortion (or cognitive error) that occurs when one takes a single negative event and makes a general rule out of it without ever testing this rule. A single negative event is viewed as the norm. For example, 'I made a mistake, therefore I'm incompetent to do my job.' Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 911.

questions.question_text: Strongest learning occurs when the delay is
questions.explanation: Longer the interval, poorer the learning.

questions.question_text: According to Ebbinghaus curve, there is a sharp drop in forgetting over
questions.explanation: The Ebbinghaus curve is a graph depicting the rate of forgetting of information. The amount of learned material – originally the number of nonsense syllables – remembered is plotted on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis. There is a sharp drop in forgetting over the first nine hours. After nine hours, the rate of forgetting slows and declines little thereafter, even after the lapse of 31 days. The main findings from his and other studies are: Forgetting is maximum in the first few hours and the rate of forgetting gets less with time; Forgetting is never complete and some information is retained over longer periods of time, even for life; Recalling the material during the test period increases the probability of remembering items or events; Continuous motor skills such as cycling and swimming etc show no forgetting at all, but discrete motors skills such as typing are lost more quickly. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015. Davis RL, Zhong Y. The biology of forgetting—a perspective. Neuron. 2017 Aug 2;95(3):490-503.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man was admitted to the acquired brain injury unit with severe memory impairment. Which of the common clinical tests can be used to test his immediate memory?

options.text: Recall of recent topics in news

questions.explanation: The terms used in psychology and psychiatry are somewhat different which could lead to some confusion. The terms used in psychology are short term memory (immediate memory in psychiatry) and long-term memory (recent memory and remote memory in psychiatry). Digit span tests immediate memory (STM). Recollection of a name and an address after 5 minutes is seen as a test of recent memory (which, in fact, is a part of LTM and should not be considered as a test of STM)

questions.question_text: A group of subjects studying molecular biology were asked to answer multiple choice questions. What mode of retrieval is this?
questions.explanation: Modes of retrieval (LTM transferred onto STM) are through 1.Recognition (solving MCQs) 2.Recall (actively searching and reproducing), 3.Reintegration/reconstruction (recollection of past experiences based on certain cues). An eyewitness testimony is a reconstructive memory, which is a mode of retrieval from long-term memory. However, a reconstructive memory of events as in eyewitness testimony is affected by the type of questioning asked to elicit the memory.

questions.question_text: A child was told to finish homework tasks before he can play outside. This is based on
questions.explanation: The Premack principle asserts that access to a preferred action will reinforce any action that is less preferred. Any behaviour that is preferred to a second behaviour will theoretically reinforce the second behaviour. This is what grandmothers do when they say "eat the spinach, and I will then give you a candy". Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1019.

questions.question_text: Mr. Z was admitted to a neuropsychiatric unit with a diagnosis of an amnesic syndrome. He was referred to psychology for psychometric testing. Which of the following would be unimpaired in formal testing?
questions.explanation: Various disorders can give rise to amnesic syndromes (E.g. hypoxia, herpes encephalitis) and the features would include 1. Unimpaired immediate memory. 2. The presence of anterograde amnesia-inability to acquire new information (impaired delayed recall) 3. The presence of retrograde amnesia of variable extent and severity 4. Unimpaired global intellectual abilities 5. Unimpaired implicit memory

questions.question_text: Choose the most unstructured test from the following list
questions.explanation: The Rorschach test consists of 10 ambiguous symmetrical inkblots. The examiner writes down verbatim what the patient says during the 'free-association' or 'response proper' phase. An almost unlimited range of responses is possible with the Rorschach test. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 59.

questions.question_text: A psychologist performed paired associates test on a 71-year-old man complaining of memory loss. This test is useful to check
questions.explanation: Verbal paired associates evaluates verbal memory for word pairs. After 10 or 14 word pairs are read aloud to the examinee, the first word of each pair is read and the examinee is asked to provide the associated word. There is a delayed recall and recognition condition in the Wechsler Memory Scale. Ref: Hodges JR. Cognitive assessment for clinicians, 3rd Edition. 2018. pp. 257-258.

questions.question_text: Mr. Y is admitted to a medical ward with a diagnosis of delirium. The cognitive deficit that is characteristic of delirium is
questions.explanation: Delirium occurs in many hospitalized older patients and has serious consequences including increased risk for death and admission to long-term care. Impaired attention is the cardinal feature of delirium.

questions.question_text: A socio-psychological approach is adopted by which of the following theories of motivation?
questions.explanation: The Homeostatic drive theory (Cannon), Drive reduction theory (Hull) and Arousal reduction theory (Hebb) are all based on biopsychological perspective, which examines the physiological motives such as hunger, thirst etc in humans and animals. They are also called as extrinsic motivation theories. The Needs theory and Goal theory, also called intrinsic motivation theories, are based on socio-psychological approach which addresses the cognitive motives behind people's complex behaviour in the context of their social situations such as work, family and society. Maslow's Hierarchy of needs is based on the humanistic approach that tries to explain why people strive to achieve higher and higher goals in an attempt to attain self-fulfillment.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following refers to the act of bringing past experiences as they happened into conscious awareness?
questions.explanation: The process of recalling an entire memory from a partial cue, like remembering a speech upon hearing the first few words, is called reintegration.

questions.question_text: Mr. X mentioned that he has vivid memories of where he was, what he was doing and was even able to remember other fine details, when he heard the news of suicide bombing of the twin towers in 2001. These memories have been termed as
questions.explanation: Flashbulb memories are a specific type of autobiographical memory in which the person becomes aware of an emotionally arousing event, for example, the 9/11 terrorist bombings. Even though they are recalled with seeming accuracy due to rehearsal, their accuracy cannot be assumed. Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish's clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 63.

questions.question_text: In the alcoholic blackouts, the following type of memory loss is seen

options.text: Anterograde amnesia due to failure to consolidation
Anterograde amnesia due to failure to recall

correct_answer.text: Anterograde amnesia due to failure to consolidation

correct_answers.text: Anterograde amnesia due to failure to consolidation

questions.explanation: Alcohol-induced amnesia ('blackouts' or 'palimpsest') is characterised by discrete episodes of anterograde amnesia that occur in association with alcohol intoxication. Patients will report a gap in their memory lasting for several hours, with global or partial amnesia for their actions during that time. The patient's behaviour is usually characteristic of their normal behaviour when intoxicated. There is a breakdown in transfer of information from short-term to long-term storage; occurs while immediate (very brief short-term) and remote (long-term; formed prior to intoxication) memory abilities remain intact. Alcohol blocks the consolidation of new memories into old memories, a process that is thought to involve the hippocampus and related temporal lobe structures. Alcohol facilitates faster forgetting. Rapid forgetting is a hallmark of hippocampal dysfunction. Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 600. Hermens DF, Lagopoulos J. Binge drinking and the young brain: A mini review of the neurobiological underpinnings of alcohol-induced blackout. Frontiers in psychology. 2018 Jan 19;9:12. Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 277-278.

questions.question_text: Situation specific amnesia may arise in all of the following situations except

options.text: Being the victim of an offence
Being the victim of childhood sexual abuse

questions.explanation: Situation specific amnesia has not been reported in patients with adjustment disorder. Offenders as well as victims of crimes commonly claim amnesia regarding the offence. Cross sectional studies have found that in 25-45% of homicides, 8% of other violent crimes and a small percentage of non-violent crimes, offenders claim for the offence (Kopelman 2002a). Amnesia for an offence can also occur in alcohol intoxication, substance misuse and acute psychosis but purely psychological amnesia occurs most commonly in crimes of passion. In people with PTSD Anterograde memory dysfunction has been demonstrated in people with PTSD and there are claims that they have a loss of hippocampal volume on MRI (Bremmer 1999), which has been attributed to effects of glucocorticoids (Markowitsch 1996). (Excerpt from Psychogenic amnesia, http://apt.rcpsych.org/content/15/2/152 (accessed April 13, 2015)).

questions.question_text: The principle of combining separate pieces of information into one meaningful combination is called
questions.explanation: Chunking is the recoding of smaller units of information into larger, familiar units. Miller proposed that chunking is achieved by grouping or organising a sequence of inputs and recoding it with a concise name. Chunking is assumed to help by bypassing the limited capacity of working memory. For example the numbers 1,5,2,3,5,2,5,8,5,3,7,8 would normally overload our short term memory but if they are arranged into chunks 152, 352, 585, 378, they become a lot more manageable. The capacity of STM according to Miller is 7+/- 2, as evident while testing digit span. By chunking, larger information could be sorted into 7+/- 2 items and effectively stored. Ref: Thalmann M et al. How does chunking help working memory?. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition. 2019 Jan;45(1):37.

questions.question_text: A Lotto player thinks that more he loses, the more chances that he wins later. So he keeps playing the Lotto. This is best described as
questions.explanation: Gambler's fallacy is the false belief that the probability of an event in a random sequence is dependent on preceding events, its probability increasing with each successive occasion on which it fails to occur. Thus, if black has come up many times in succession at a roulette table, a false belief may develop that red is increasingly likely on each subsequent spin of the wheel, to even out the sequence in the long run; or if a fair coin is tossed repeatedly and tails comes up many times in a row, a gambler may believe that heads is more likely on the following toss. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following statements is true about classical conditioning?

options.text: Classical conditioning occurs when a new stimulus is repeatedly paired with a conditioned stimulus
Classical conditioning was first demonstrated by Skinner
Classical conditioning takes place irrespective of the nature of the unconditioned stimulus
Classical conditioning is a slow process depending on repeated presentations of the stimulus
In classical conditioning, the responses are often autonomic

correct_answer.text: In classical conditioning, the responses are often autonomic

correct_answers.text: In classical conditioning, the responses are often autonomic

questions.explanation: Classical conditioning was first described by Ivan Pavlov. It occurs when an initially neutral stimulus, such as ticking of a metronome, comes to elicit a particular response, such as salivation, as a consequence of being paired repeatedly with an unconditioned stimulus, such as food. In classical conditioning, the responses are often autonomic (e.g. salivation, change in heart rate). Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1014. Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015. p. 135.

questions.question_text: A fear of spiders extending itself to a fear of other insects is an example of what behavioural phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Stimulus generalisation is the tendency for a learned response to a particular stimulus to be elicited by other stimuli that resemble it. A generalisation gradient can be drawn up showing that the more similar the stimuli, the more similar the responses. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: The most important and common bedside test that is used in demonstrating age-associated memory impairment would be
questions.explanation: Approximately 40% of individuals aged 65 and over show AAMI. Cognitive testing has demonstrated that memory for non-verbal material seems to be more affected by aging than memory for verbal material, and delayed recall is more affected than immediate recall. Here the subject is given a list of 20 words and then ask him or her to recall as many as possible in 20 minutes. Finally, the score is compared with standardised scores for the given age.

questions.question_text: A 59-year-old man played Lotto consistently with the desire to win big one day. He has won small amounts of money on certain occasions. What is the reinforcement schedule demonstrated by his behaviour?
questions.explanation: In operant conditioning, a variable-ratio schedule is one in which a reward is delivered after the organism has made a random number of responses, and is then rewarded after a further random number of responses, and so on. Ratio schedules, especially variable ratio schedules, can generate high rates of behaviour, as seen in the behaviour directed at a casino slot machine. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015. Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1018.

questions.question_text: Wechsler Adult intelligence scales (WAIS-R) are for people
questions.explanation: Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scales are for people aged 16 and over. Wechsler Intelligence Scales for Children are for those aged 6 to 16 years. Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scales of Intelligence are for 3 to 7 year-old children. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 82.

questions.question_text: In a scientific experiment, a neutral stimulus (a bell) is paired with a stimulus (food) that produces an autonomic response (salivation). Which of the following learning mechanisms has been employed?
questions.explanation: In Pavlov's experiments the food is the unconditioned stimulus because it unconditionally elicits salivation before the experiment begins. The bell is known as the conditioned stimulus because it only elicits the salivary response conditional on the food-bell pairings. Forward conditioning is the usual method of classical conditioning, in which the conditioned stimulus precedes the unconditioned stimulus. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1014. Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Intelligent behaviours arise from a balance between analytical, creative and physical abilities. This notion refers to which of the following?
questions.explanation: Robert Sternberg's triarchic theory of successful intelligence contends that intelligent behaviour arises from a balance between analytical, creative, and practical abilities. These abilities function collectively to allow individuals to achieve success within particular sociocultural contexts. Ref: Saw KN, Han B. Effectiveness of successful intelligence training program: A meta‐analysis. PsyCh Journal. 2021 Apr 18.

questions.question_text: Which of the following psychological theories is not concerned with the faculties of memory and forgetting?
questions.explanation: Abraham Maslow proposed a need-hierarchy theory (not a theory of memory). According to Maslow, the strongest and most imperative are the physiological needs for food, water, oxygen, and sex. If the physiological needs are gratified, the needs for safety emerge, and the person begins to seek out safe environments. Next to emerge are needs for love and belonging, and the person yearns for a friend, a lover, a place in a group. Then needs for esteem come to the fore, and the person seeks self-respect, respect from others, status, and achievement. Then last, usually only if all the others have been reasonably well-satisfied, there emerges a need for self-actualisation. Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.
